::: {.callout-note .se-question appearance="simple"}
## The question

[Finding the area of surface obtained by rotating $(x-a)^2 + (y-b)^2 = r^2, 0 < r < a$, about the line $x = -a$.](https://math.stackexchange.com/questions/3218161/finding-the-area-of-surface-obtained-by-rotating-x-a2-y-b2-r2-0-r), asked by [Hellowhatsup](https://math.stackexchange.com/users/657337/hellowhatsup) on Mathematics Stack Exchange (2019-05-08; [CC BY-SA 4.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/)):

> So I solved this problem by using parametric euqations, where x= a + r cos t and y = a  +r sin t. Then got the answer 8$\pi r^2a$. But the answer sheet keeps saying that it is 16$\pi ra$. I'm not sure who's right.
>
> [![enter image description here][q-1]][q-1]
>
>
>   [q-1]: UOI3w.jpg
:::

[Pappus's Centroid Theorem](http://mathworld.wolfram.com/PappussCentroidTheorem.html) says that the area of a surface of revolution is equal to the length of the rotated curve times the distance the centroid travels.

In this case the rotated curve is a circle, and its circumference is $2\pi r$.  The centroid of the circle is the center $(a,b)$.  It travels around a circle of radius $2a$, for a distance of $2\pi(2a) = 4\pi a$.

Therefore the surface area is $(2\pi r)(4\pi a) = 8 \pi^2 r a$.
